## Overview

The Karankawa were an Indigenous group concentrated in southern Texas along the coast of the Gulf of Mexico, especially in the lower Colorado River and Brazos River valleys. They consisted of several independent, seasonal semi-nomadic groups that shared a language and some cultural practices. Their movements connected the mainland, coastal waters, and barrier islands. They travelled in dugout canoes, hunted and gathered along rivers and shores, and maintained trade with inland groups. European colonization brought violent encounters, forced displacement, and attacks on Karankawa settlements. By 1891, the Karankawa had ceased to exist as a functioning tribe, although unrecognized tribes claim Karankawa descent. Their extinct language is unclassified and may have been a language isolate.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

Men wore hide breechcloths, while women wore deerhide skirts. Neither men nor women wore headcovers or shoes. Some women obtained European clothing, but they either tore it apart or wore it temporarily. European blankets were more useful and were fastened to the body during cold weather, sometimes with thorns. Both men and women wore a small bracelet of undressed deer skin. Children in the warm climate did not wear clothing until they were about 10 years old.

Karankawa people practiced forehead flattening. A baby’s forehead was shaped with a piece of cloth, a thin board, and a wadded cloth, each tied to the head with a bandage and left in place for about one year. Men and women also rubbed sharks’ oil over their bodies to deter mosquitoes and keep the skin soft. Men wore their long hair braided with three strands and inserted bright items such as ribbons or colored flannel. Women did not braid their hair or comb it regularly.

### Architecture

Karankawa campsites were always close to the shoreline of a nearby body of water. The people constructed dwellings by arranging willow branches in a circle, bending the tops toward the centre, and interlocking them in wickerwork. The framework was fastened with deerskin. Deer, wildcat, panther, or bear skins were placed over it and secured with deer-hide thongs. The sources call these dwellings wigwams, or *ba'ak* in the Karankawa language. A fire was made in the centre and kept burning day and night. Animal hides and pelts were used for sitting and sleeping.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Karankawa household goods and utensils included wooden spoons, ceramic vessels, fishbone needles, and fine deer sinew. Ceramic pots were used for boiling food, and asphaltum was applied as a coating to pottery such as ollas, jars, and bowls. Asphaltum was also used to bind arrowheads to their shafts and waterproof woven baskets. Firesticks were carried in a package secured with deer-hide thongs. The people travelled in dugout canoes made from large trees with the bark left intact; after European contact, old skiffs obtained from settlers were also called *awa'n*.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The Karankawa practiced tattooing. Described tattoos included a blue circle over each cheekbone, a horizontal blue line from the outer corner of the eye toward the ear, three parallel perpendicular lines on the chin, and two additional lines extending downward from beneath the corners of the mouth. European explorers also described labrets, or cane piercings, on the lower lips, nose, and other parts of the body.

Women wore no ornaments, while men wore necklaces of small shells, glass beads, pistachios, and thin metal disks around the throat. Men also wore finger rings and braided bright items into their hair. Both men and women wore small bracelets of undressed deer skin.

## Music & performance

The Karankawa possessed at least three musical instruments. One was a large gourd filled with stones and shaken to produce sound. Another was a fluted piece of wood over which a stick was drawn. The third was a flute that was softly blown.

Music also formed part of a ceremony held at the full moon and after very successful hunting or fishing expeditions. The Karankawa gathered around a central fire and prepared a strong, bitter brew from yaupon leaves. One person stood within the circle of men, wrapped in skins up to the head, and bent over while walking around the fire. The participants chanted in chromatic ascending and descending tones, and everyone joined the chorus. The ceremony continued throughout the night.

The Karankawa also used smoke signals for long-distance communication. The smoke from a small fire could be made to rise in different ways, and these signals were intelligible to them across long distances.

## Dance & theatre

They describe a nocturnal ceremony involving movement around a central fire, chanting, and a participant wrapped in skins.

## Festivals & rituals

They record a ceremony held at the full moon and after especially successful hunting or fishing expeditions. Participants gathered around a central fire, prepared and drank a yaupon brew, chanted, and continued the ceremony through the night.

Information about religious beliefs was limited because the Karankawa did not reveal the purposes of their actions or their beliefs. When questioned about religion, they pointed at the sky. They stared at the sun when it disappeared into the sea, smoked tobacco through their nostrils toward the north, east, west, and south, and whistled at certain times for purposes that remained unknown.

Burial practices included wrapping the corpse in a prepared buffalo hide and burying the person with a club, bow, arrows, smoked meat, corn, vegetables, and two pieces of rock used instead of flint for making fire. The sources associate these grave goods with the belief that the dead person would use them after waking.

Marriage included bride price and bride service. In the described service, the husband gave the food he collected or hunted to his wife, who delivered it to her parents and received food to return to him. The sources also describe divorce as common in marriages without children and patrilocal residence after the marriage ritual.

## Foodways

Karankawa cuisine included venison, rabbit, fowl, fish, turtles, oysters, and other shellfish. Wild foods included berries, persimmons, wild grapes, sea-bird eggs, tuna, nopales, and nuts. Nopales were identified as prickly pear cactus fruit and paddles. Food was boiled in ceramic pots or roasted over an open fire, and dishes were seasoned with chile.

After European contact, the Karankawa made bread from imported wheat flour. They placed the dough on a flat stone and baked it over an open fire. They also drank imported sweet coffee. Karankawa cooks were described as skilled at obtaining pure, fresh water, even though white settlers’ wells had a brackish taste.

Archaeological evidence from seasonal campsites indicates a coastal subsistence pattern involving fishing, shellfish harvesting, and the seasonal hunting of deer and bison. The sources also discuss historical claims of cannibalism. Modern anthropology, ethnohistory, and archaeology generally characterize widespread or dietary cannibalism as a colonial misconception, while some colonial accounts described restricted, ritualistic warfare practices.

## Oral tradition & literature

They state that little is known of the extinct Karankawa language, although a couple hundred words were preserved from collections made in 1698, 1720, and 1828, with three additional lists collected in the 1880s from non-Karankawa who knew some words.

Historical accounts include testimony attributed to Jean-Baptiste Talon and reports by Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca. These records describe aspects of Karankawa life, warfare, burial, food, and relations with Europeans, but they are colonial and ethnographic accounts rather than Karankawa literary works.

## Language & religion

Karankawa is an extinct, unclassified language of the Texas coast. It was not closely related to other known languages in the area and may have been a language isolate. It has sometimes been placed within a Coahuiltecan family, but that classification is described as spurious. Only a few hundred words survive. The recorded vocabulary includes *Kaup(ě)n* “Speak,” *Yamawe* “Man,” *Kaninma* “Woman” or “Mother,” *Glle-i* “Water,” *Ahayika* “Friend,” *Dōwal* “Sun,” *Kiss* “Dog,” *Aknamus* “Eat,” and *Ye* “Go” or “Walk.”

The Karankawa also possessed a gesture language for communicating with people from other Native American tribes. Their religious beliefs were only partly recorded. Europeans observed ceremonies involving yaupon, fire, chanting, tobacco, the sun, and burial goods, but the purposes of many actions remained unknown.
